intro.text: Almost every real web app needs accounts: a way for people to sign up, log in, and see only their own data. This chapter covers the two ideas behind that — authentication (proving who you are: sign-up, login, and the token flow that keeps users signed in) and authorization (deciding what each signed-in user is allowed to touch). We stay at the concept level here: the goal is to understand the machinery well enough to direct auth work, ask the right security questions, and recognize when protection is missing.

lessons.title: How User Authentication Works
lessons.objective: Understand how user authentication features like login and sign-up actually work under the hood. You'll learn the core flow of token-based authentication well enough to direct the AI's auth work, ask the right security questions, and figure out the cause when something goes wrong.

blocks.text: Sign-up creates an account using information such as an email address and password. An authentication service such as Supabase Auth handles password hashing and account verification; the app should not store plain-text passwords in its own data tables.
Login is the process of proving you're the same person who signed up. Here's the flow:
The browser sends the email and password the user typed in to the server.
The server checks whether they match the credentials stored in the database.
If they match, the server issues a token — think of it as an entry ticket — and hands it back to the browser.
For requests that need authentication, the app sends the appropriate access token so the server can verify the session.
The token even carries ID information that identifies the user, so the server can tell directly whose request it's looking at.

steps.title: So what exactly is a token?

blocks.text: A token is a digital entry pass issued by the server. It's usually a long string that looks like random characters, and inside it carries information that identifies the user — like a user ID — plus a signature that prevents forgery and tampering.
For a signed token such as a JWT, the server validates the signature, expiration, and relevant claims. Authorization checks still decide which data the request may access.
“A token is a little ID card that tells the server whose request this is.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

blocks.text: Because a token is the entry pass, the moment someone steals it they can impersonate the user. If a hacker gets hold of just the token, they can access your account — no password needed — and view or manipulate your data. It's the most critical failure mode in an authentication system, and the reason a manager can never wave auth work through on the AI's say-so alone.
Access tokens have a limited lifetime set by the authentication system. Shorter lifetimes reduce how long a stolen token can be used, but the exact duration varies.
A refresh mechanism can maintain a session without asking the user to sign in every time an access token expires.
To avoid making users log in constantly because of short lifetimes, servers issue two kinds of tokens together:
Access token: the entry pass used when accessing the service. Short lifetime.
Refresh token: a special token used to get a new access token issued. Usually single-use.
When the access token expires, the browser uses the refresh token to get a fresh access token — so you keep using the service without interruption.

lessons.title: Understanding Authorization to Protect Your Data
lessons.objective: Understand why authentication by itself cannot keep your data safe, learn the concept of authorization — controlling who may access which data — well enough to notice when it's been skipped, and know the role of Supabase's RLS feature so you can ask for it by name.

blocks.text: Authentication confirms an identity. It does not by itself establish which database rows that user may read or change. Access depends on the permissions and policies that are configured.

Suppose Alex signs in and requests Jordan’s links. If the database grants that request and no policy restricts it to the owner, the data could be exposed. A correct ownership policy should prevent that access.

blocks.title: Before you continue
blocks.text: A valid login token proves identity, not ownership. Check the database permissions and row-level policies before treating an app as protected.

Authorization is the step that comes after authentication: whenever a user tries to access a specific piece of data, the system additionally checks whether that user actually has permission for that data. A campus analogy makes the difference easy to remember:
Authentication — the check at the campus gate: are you a student or an instructor who's allowed to enter the school at all?
Authorization — the check at the faculty office door: is the person trying to walk in actually a professor?
Both checks matter. Getting through the front gate (logging in) should never automatically open every door inside the building (every row in your database).

So that you can set up authorization without pain, Supabase provides a feature called RLS (Row Level Security). True to its name, it lets you attach access rules to each individual row of a table. That means you can create policies like “Jordan's rows can only be accessed by Jordan” and “Alex's rows can only be accessed by Alex.”
RLS policies can govern SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE separately. Review every operation your app needs; an operation with no applicable permission should remain denied.
